## Abstract

A machine-learning soil map returns a number at every pixel. It rarely
returns an *honest* interval around that number, because the residual
spatial structure the model failed to explain is treated as noise
rather than as a signal with a covariance. Pillar 7 takes the opposite
route: it puts the spatial dependence *inside* the model, as a Gaussian
process random effect, and returns a full posterior over every quantity
of interest [@Banerjee2014hierarchical; @Cressie2011].

This vignette derives the hierarchy, is explicit about the one
non-conjugate parameter and the concession `edaphos` makes for it, and
then spends most of its length on the part that is usually skipped: the
two diagnostics that decide whether the fitted spatial field means
anything at all.

## 1. The hierarchy

Write the observed soil property at site $s_i$ as a mean structure plus
a spatially correlated random effect plus independent error:

$$
y(s_i) \;=\; \mathbf{x}(s_i)^\top \boldsymbol\beta \;+\; w(s_i) \;+\; \varepsilon(s_i),
\qquad i = 1,\dots,n .
$$

The three layers are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{data:} \quad & y \mid \boldsymbol\beta, w, \tau^2 \;\sim\; N(X\boldsymbol\beta + w,\; \tau^2 I) \\
\text{process:} \quad & w \mid \sigma^2, \phi \;\sim\; N(0,\; \sigma^2 R(\phi)) \\
\text{priors:} \quad & \boldsymbol\beta \sim N(0, v_\beta I), \quad
                       \sigma^2 \sim IG(a, b), \quad \tau^2 \sim IG(a, b)
\end{aligned}
$$

with an exponential correlation function

$$
R(\phi)_{ij} \;=\; \exp\!\big(-\phi \, \lVert s_i - s_j \rVert\big).
$$

Note the parameterisation carefully, because it is the source of most
mistakes with this model: **$\phi$ is a decay rate, not a range.** Its
units are 1/distance. *Large* $\phi$ means correlation dies off
quickly; $\phi \to \infty$ drives $R \to I$. The practical correlation
range is roughly $3/\phi$. If your coordinates are in degrees, a
sensible $\phi$ is a very different number than if they are in metres.

$\tau^2$ is the **nugget**: variation below the shortest sampling
distance, pooling laboratory error and micro-scale heterogeneity.
$\sigma^2$ is the **partial sill**, the variance of the structured
field.

### 1.1 Why $\phi$ is the hard one

Collapse $w$ out of the likelihood:

$$
y \mid \boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2, \tau^2, \phi \;\sim\;
N\!\left(X\boldsymbol\beta,\; \Sigma\right),
\qquad \Sigma = \sigma^2 R(\phi) + \tau^2 I .
$$

Conditional on $\phi$ this is an ordinary Bayesian linear model with a
known covariance: $\boldsymbol\beta$ has a Gaussian full conditional
and the variances have inverse-gamma full conditionals. Every update is
closed-form.

But $\phi$ sits *inside a matrix inverse and a determinant*. It has no
conjugate update, and a Metropolis step on it pays an $O(n^3)$ Cholesky
for every proposal, accepted or rejected.

`edaphos` avoids the Metropolis step. It **profiles** $\phi$: over the
bracket `phi_range` it maximises the marginal likelihood once, fixes
$\phi$ at $\hat\phi$, and runs a fully conjugate Gibbs sampler for
everything else. This is the concession INLA makes for its
hyperparameters [@Rue2009inla] — treat the rate as estimated rather
than sampled, buy exact fast updates for the parameters you report.

The cost, stated plainly: the reported posterior for
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is *conditional on* $\hat\phi$ and does not
propagate uncertainty in the rate. It is a conditional posterior, not a
joint one.

## 2. The Cerrado grid

`br_cerrado` is a 45 × 45 regular grid of synthesised Cerrado
observations bundled with the package, so this vignette runs offline
and identically everywhere.

```{r data}
data(br_cerrado)
str(br_cerrado)
```

```{r subsample}
set.seed(42)
idx   <- sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 220)
train <- br_cerrado[idx, ]
test  <- br_cerrado[-idx, ][sample(nrow(br_cerrado) - 220, 200), ]

c(n_train = nrow(train), n_test = nrow(test))
```

The Gibbs sampler is $O(n^3)$ per iteration through the Cholesky, so
$n$ — not the iteration count — is what binds on a laptop.

## 3. Fit the full model, and read the warning

```{r fit-full}
fit_full <- bhs_fit(
  data      = train,
  formula   = soc ~ elev + slope + twi + map_mm,
  coords    = c("x", "y"),
  backend   = "gibbs",
  nmcmc     = 1500L, burn = 500L, thin = 2L,
  phi_range = c(0.05, 1000),
  seed      = 1L, verbose = FALSE
)
```

That warning is not noise to be silenced. It is the first diagnostic.

`bhs_fit()` warns when $\hat\phi$ lands on an endpoint of
`phi_range`, because then the *bracket* — not the data — determined the
answer. Here the likelihood is still climbing at the upper end: it
wants $\phi$ as large as it can get, which is the model's way of saying
**there is no residual spatial structure left to fit**. Every driver of
`soc` in this synthesised grid is already in the formula, so the
residual is white.

Widening the bracket will not help; it will rail again, further out.
The right conclusion is that a spatial random effect is not needed for
this specification.

### 3.1 The diagnostic that works, and the one that does not

The number most often quoted from a fit like this is the spatial
fraction $\sigma^2 / (\sigma^2 + \tau^2)$. This section shows why, on
its own, it tells you nothing.

The question a spatial model has to answer first is whether the fitted
correlation is *resolvable by the sampling design at all*. The
practical range is $3/\phi$; compare it to the shortest distance
between two sampled sites:

```{r aliased}
d_min <- min(dist(train[, c("x", "y")]))

c(phi_hat       = fit_full$phi_hat,
  range_3_over  = 3 / fit_full$phi_hat,
  d_min         = d_min,
  range_per_dmin = (3 / fit_full$phi_hat) / d_min,
  corr_nearest  = exp(-fit_full$phi_hat * d_min))
```

The fitted range is *shorter than the gap between the two closest
observations*. Nothing in the design can see structure at that scale:
even nearest neighbours are essentially uncorrelated, so $R$ is
numerically the identity and
$\Sigma = \sigma^2 R + \tau^2 I \approx (\sigma^2 + \tau^2) I$. In that
regime $w$ and $\varepsilon$ enter the likelihood identically — they
are **aliased**, and only their sum is a statement about the data.

Now look at the spatial fraction anyway:

```{r frac-full}
fr_full <- fit_full$sigma2_draws /
           (fit_full$sigma2_draws + fit_full$tau2_draws)
c(mean = mean(fr_full), sd = sd(fr_full))
```

Near 1, with a tight posterior — which reads as "almost all residual
variance is spatially structured" and is the opposite of the truth.
The apparent precision is the trap: a narrow posterior on an aliased
quantity is not evidence. Section 4 fits a model where the field *is*
real and shows this same number barely moves, which is the point.

## 4. Omit a driver, and the field reappears

A GP random effect is, operationally, a *surrogate for spatially smooth
predictors you do not have*. We can demonstrate that directly by
dropping `map_mm` — a smooth climate driver — and refitting.

```{r fit-drop}
fit_drop <- bhs_fit(
  data      = train,
  formula   = soc ~ elev + slope + twi,
  coords    = c("x", "y"),
  backend   = "gibbs",
  nmcmc     = 1500L, burn = 500L, thin = 2L,
  phi_range = c(0.05, 1000),
  seed      = 1L, verbose = FALSE
)

c(phi_hat        = fit_drop$phi_hat,
  interior       = fit_drop$phi_hat < 1000,
  range_3_over   = 3 / fit_drop$phi_hat,
  range_per_dmin = (3 / fit_drop$phi_hat) / d_min,
  corr_nearest   = exp(-fit_drop$phi_hat * d_min))
```

No warning this time: $\hat\phi$ is interior, so the data — not the
bracket — chose it. And the range now spans several nearest-neighbour
spacings, with immediate neighbours meaningfully correlated. This is a
real, short-range field: the GP has taken over the job the omitted
rainfall covariate was doing.

That is the honest interpretation of a spatial random effect in any
applied fit — it is as much a statement about what is *missing* from
your covariate stack as about pedogenesis.

Now the promised comparison. Here is the spatial fraction for this
fit, where the field is genuine:

```{r frac-drop}
fr_drop <- fit_drop$sigma2_draws /
           (fit_drop$sigma2_draws + fit_drop$tau2_draws)

rbind(`full (no resolvable field)` = c(mean = mean(fr_full), sd = sd(fr_full)),
      `reduced (real field)`       = c(mean = mean(fr_drop), sd = sd(fr_drop)))
```

The two are practically indistinguishable — same value, same tight
posterior — yet one fit has a resolvable spatial field and the other
has none. **The spatial fraction did not detect the difference.** What
did was $\hat\phi$: interior versus railed, and its range measured
against the sampling distance.

Report those together, or report neither.

```{r beta}
round(t(apply(fit_drop$beta_draws, 2, function(b)
  c(mean = mean(b), sd = sd(b),
    q025 = quantile(b, 0.025, names = FALSE),
    q975 = quantile(b, 0.975, names = FALSE)))), 4)
```

A coefficient whose 95% credible interval excludes zero is one the data
resolve *after* the field has absorbed everything it can — a stricter
bar than an OLS $p$-value, because a covariate that merely happens to
be smooth in space will have its apparent effect soaked up by $w$.

## 5. Bayesian kriging, and whether the interval is earned

Prediction at a new site is *not* $\mathbf{x}_0^\top
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$. Marginalising the field out of the hierarchy
gives the exact Gaussian conditional

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[y_0 \mid y] &= \mathbf{x}_0^\top \boldsymbol\beta
  + \sigma^2 \mathbf{r}_0^\top \Sigma^{-1} (y - X\boldsymbol\beta), \\
V[y_0 \mid y] &= \underbrace{\sigma^2 + \tau^2}_{\text{marginal}}
  - \underbrace{\sigma^4 \mathbf{r}_0^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{r}_0}_{\text{kriging variance}},
\end{aligned}
$$

evaluated at every retained posterior draw of
$(\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2, \tau^2)$.

The second variance term is what makes the interval location-aware. It
is largest — so the subtraction is largest, so the interval is
narrowest — at sites surrounded by data, and it vanishes as
$\mathbf{r}_0 \to 0$, correctly relaxing the predictive variance to the
full marginal $\sigma^2 + \tau^2$ far from any observation. You can
watch both limits:

```{r variance-limits}
p_at  <- predict(fit_drop, newdata = train, n_draws = 1000L)  # on the data
far   <- test[1:50, ];  far$x <- far$x + 500                  # far outside
p_far <- predict(fit_drop, newdata = far, n_draws = 1000L)

s2 <- mean(fit_drop$sigma2_draws); t2 <- mean(fit_drop$tau2_draws)
c(sd_at_observed = mean(p_at$sd),
  sd_far_away    = mean(p_far$sd),
  sqrt_marginal  = sqrt(s2 + t2))
```

`sd_far_away` should land on `sqrt_marginal`, and `sd_at_observed`
should sit well below it. An implementation that adds only the nugget
would return the *same* small number in both columns — narrow intervals
everywhere, including where the model knows nothing.

### 5.1 Coverage

```{r coverage}
pred    <- predict(fit_drop, newdata = test)
covered <- test$soc >= pred$q025 & test$soc <= pred$q975

c(picp_95    = mean(covered),
  mean_width = mean(pred$q975 - pred$q025),
  rmse       = sqrt(mean((test$soc - pred$mean)^2)),
  r2         = 1 - sum((test$soc - pred$mean)^2) /
                   sum((test$soc - mean(train$soc))^2))
```

Read coverage and width together, never separately. An interval from
$-\infty$ to $\infty$ has perfect coverage; a degenerate one has
perfect width. A model earns trust when coverage lands near nominal
*while* the width stays narrow enough to inform a decision.

Note the $R^2$ denominator: the **training** mean, not the test-set
mean. Scoring against the test mean measures the model against an
oracle no deployed map has, and inflates $R^2$ for free.

## 6. Where this connects

`bhs_fit()` returns an object the package's unified uncertainty layer
understands, so the same calibration diagnostic applies here as to
every other pillar:

```{r posterior-class}
post <- as_edaphos_posterior(fit_drop)
class(post)
```

See `vignette("uncertainty-unified")` for the cross-pillar comparison
and `vignette("capstone-cerrado-campaign")` for this model inside a
full sampling-campaign decision.

## 7. Limitations

- $\phi$ is profiled, not sampled (§1.1); posteriors are conditional on
  $\hat\phi$. Always check the warning before reading the variance
  split (§3.1).
- The exponential correlation is isotropic. Anisotropic pedogenesis —
  a catena down a slope — is not represented.
- The $O(n^3)$ Cholesky bounds practical $n$ to the low thousands. The
  RcppArmadillo backend moves the constant, not the exponent.
- `br_cerrado` is synthesised. The numbers above demonstrate machinery,
  not a published finding about the Cerrado. For real WoSIS profiles
  see `vignette("case-cerrado-end-to-end")`.
